formNote: The Shuowen: 聲，音也。从耳，殸聲 — “sound: from ear, with 殸 as phonetic.” 殸 is the old form of 磬, the hanging stone chime. Mojidata IDS: ⿱殸耳.
summary: Sound, voice, and tone: the same word names a noise, a person’s voice and the four tones of Middle Chinese. Buddhist translators used it for the śrāvaka, the disciple who hears the teaching’s voice.
placement: Low on the left, below 如: sound, under the saying. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: The Chime and the Ear
satellites.evidence: 聲 is 殸 over 耳 (Mojidata IDS): the stone chime and the ear. The Shuowen reads 耳 as the meaning and 殸 as the sound, so the graph pairs a struck stone with the one who hears it.

satellites.title: 聲聞: Those Who Hear the Voice
satellites.evidence: Śrāvaka, “hearer”, from śru, “to hear”, is rendered 聲聞, “voice-hearer”: the disciple who hears the Buddha’s voice. The Chinese adds the voice that the Sanskrit leaves implied.

satellites.title: The Four Tones
satellites.evidence: In the Southern Qi, scholars led by Shen Yue named the four tones of Middle Chinese: 平 level, 上 rising, 去 departing, 入 entering. The Guangyun (1008) arranges every syllable by them. 聲 is also the word for a tone.
satellites.caveat: The attribution to Shen Yue is traditional; his treatise on the tones is lost.
